text:
You will sort 17 short lessons into homes. The homes are listed below, each with a name and a one-sentence definition.

For each lesson, choose one main home from the list. You may also choose one second home from the list, different from the main home, if the lesson belongs there too; if not, write none. Use the home names exactly as written.

Homes:
- gate: A mandatory decision point that allows work to continue only when specified criteria are met.
- tool: A reusable aid or instrument the team uses to perform recurring work consistently.
- check: A verification step that confirms required conditions, quality, or completeness before proceeding.
- judgment: A home for guidance on making decisions that depend on context, interpretation, or discretion.
- harness: A guiding structure that constrains or supports how work is performed to prevent drift or harm.
- retrieval: A stored way to locate relevant prior knowledge when it is needed.

Lessons:
L01: Read the clock every time you write a time down, because guessed times were written into records again and again, once off by two hours.
L02: When the person you work with asks for calm attention, give that and nothing else, because a technical report was given to someone who had asked only for presence.
L03: Treat an empty result, a zero, or a short list as a fact about your search, not about the world, because a crashed command printed nothing and that nothing was used as proof, and a reader that showed 5 of 321 matches never mentioned the rest.
L04: Run the one deciding check before you say "done" or "verified", because work was reported finished that had never run, and a deletion was reported that had been refused.
L05: Make a test or monitor fail once on purpose before you trust it, because one test stayed green for seven weeks for the wrong reason and a network check called a dead link healthy for more than five hours.
L06: Quote others exactly and find the real cause before naming one, because a stronger paraphrase was filed as someone else's finding, and a problem was blamed on a program because of its name.
L07: Do not trust "success", "ok", or a clean exit by itself; look at what actually landed, because a tool reported 1034 of 1034 records saved when about 767 had failed.
L08: After fixing one thing, check the things beside it, because a fix to one field left its twin broken, and the fix for that fix broke the other side.
L09: Ask a different kind of reviewer to check important work, because the most useful corrections came from the helper least like the one that erred, and from one that could only read.
L10: Before you say something is lost, check whether only its location or the reading is wrong, because a process reported dead was still running, and restarting it would have destroyed the work the alarm said was gone.
L11: Do not assume a saved change or setting is in effect until you see it act, because a switch was set that no running program ever read.
L12: State how much evidence a claim rests on, because a speed was quoted from three short chats and a rule was built on a single example.
L13: Do not rely on remembering a lesson; turn it into a step you always do, because a helper wrote a lesson down and repeated the mistake in its next message.
L14: Copy long codes and hashes with a program, never by hand, because shortened and partly invented codes were written into records several times.
L15: Say where you looked and what you found. Check another source if it could change the answer you owe the person, because files reported absent were on another branch, in another folder, or on another machine.
L16: Do not repeat a fact from notes, a summary, or a rulebook without testing it, because an accurate note quoted a number and dropped the warning beside it that the number rested on one case.
L17: Do not mark your own answer as checked unless you checked it against something outside yourself, because a model once wrote "that checks out" about a town's county and postal code with no way to look them up, and both were wrong. If you could not check, say "not checked".

Reply format. Reply with exactly one line per lesson and nothing else: no heading, no numbering, no code block, no blank answer, no extra text. Each line has this form:
LABEL | main: HOME | second: HOME or none
LABEL is the lesson's label (for example L01). After "main: " write exactly one home name copied from the list. After "second: " write exactly one other home name copied from the list, or the word none. Separate the three parts with a space, the character |, and a space. Give every label exactly once.
question_text:
For each lesson, write one sentence that answers this question: what remains judgment once this lesson has its home?

Reply format. Reply with exactly one line per lesson and nothing else: no heading, no numbering, no code block, no blank answer, no extra text. Each line has this form:
LABEL | SENTENCE
LABEL is the lesson's label (for example L01). SENTENCE is one sentence that does not contain the character |. Separate the two parts with a space, the character |, and a space. Give every label exactly once.
